questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How weather forecasters predict tropical storms
Why the Arctic is the coldest place on Earth
How climate change may make storms more dangerous
How to stay safe at home during a flood
questions.why: Phil asks how climate change is affecting extreme weather, and they focus on tropical storms.

questions.q: How does Sarah explain the difference between weather and climate?
options: Weather is what happens day to day; climate is long-term
Weather is about rain; climate is about temperature
Weather affects cities; climate affects the countryside
Weather is measured on land; climate is measured at sea
questions.why: She says weather is what you see and feel every day, while climate is more long-term.

questions.q: What does Sarah say about hurricanes, cyclones and typhoons?
options: Typhoons are the strongest and most deadly of the three
They form over cold northern seas in winter
Cyclones only happen in the Atlantic Ocean
They are one type of storm with local names
questions.why: She says they are the same; the name depends on where in the world they form.

questions.q: What do climate scientists think will happen to these storms as the world warms?
options: They will happen less often
They will cause more damage
They will move to colder regions
They will become smaller but faster
questions.why: Sarah says scientists think these storms will get more destructive as the world warms.

questions.q: According to Darren Bett, why is it a problem if storms slow down?
options: They stay longer, so there is more rain and flooding
They become much harder for forecasters to see
They grow bigger and reach many more countries
They lose their energy and turn into heavy snow
questions.why: He says a storm in the same area for longer means stronger winds and rain for longer, and more flooding.

questions.q: How are mudslides different from landslides, according to Sarah?
options: They only happen near the sea
They move more slowly and are drier
They never damage buildings
They are usually quicker and more liquid
questions.why: Sarah says mudslides tend to be faster and more liquid than landslides.

questions.q: Why does Darren mention that seas are warming and sea levels are rising?
options: To explain why storms are slowing down so much
To show that tropical storms are becoming rarer
To explain why storm surges may get more dangerous
To describe what causes landslides near the coast
questions.why: He links rising seas to storm surges, which 'could become even more dangerous'.

questions.q: What does Sarah say about the size of storm surges?
options: They are rarely more than one metre high
They can reach up to 10 metres high
They are only dangerous in rivers
They are smaller than they used to be
questions.why: Sarah says storm surges can be up to 10 metres high and can destroy buildings.
